title: DVT: Systemic Essentials & Ophthalmic Implications
summary: A comprehensive deep dive into Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT), bridging the gap between systemic vascular medicine and ophthalmic practice. This poster covers everything from Virchow's Triad to perioperative anticoagulation management in ocular surgery.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT) is the formation of a thrombus within a deep vein, most commonly in the lower extremities. While primarily a systemic condition, it serves as a critical marker for hypercoagulable states that also manifest in the eye as Retinal Vein Occlusions (RVO) and poses significant perioperative risks during ophthalmic surgery.

branches: Hypercoagulability (Factor V Leiden, Cancer, Pregnancy, OCPs)

sections.title: The Wells Criteria for DVT Probability

rows: Bedridden >3 days or major surgery <12 wks
Alternative diagnosis at least as likely

content.explanation: T: Trauma/Travel; H: Hormones (OCP/HRT); R: Relatives (Genetics); O: Old age; M: Malignancy; B: Blood disorders; O: Obesity; S: Surgery; I: Immobilization; S: Sickness (CHF/Nephrotic).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Pulmonary Embolism
content: Sudden onset Dyspnea (Shortness of breath)
Pleuritic Chest Pain
Hemoptysis (Coughing up blood)
Tachycardia (>100 bpm) and Tachypnea
Syncope or Sudden Collapse

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Flow
content: Step 1: Clinical Assessment (Wells Score calculation).
Step 2: D-dimer Assay (High sensitivity, low specificity; use to rule out in low-risk).
Step 3: Compression Ultrasonography (CUS) - Gold standard imaging.
Step 4: Venography (Rarely used now; gold standard if CUS is inconclusive).
Step 5: CT Pulmonary Angiogram (If PE is suspected).

sections.title: Perioperative Management for Ophthalmic Surgeons
content: Cataract Surgery: Continue anticoagulants (Warfarin/DOACs); risk of retrobulbar hemorrhage is minimal with topical anesthesia.
Glaucoma Surgery (Trabeculectomy): High risk of hyphema/suprachoroidal hemorrhage; consider stopping 3-5 days pre-op if systemic risk is low.
Vitreoretinal Surgery: Generally continue anticoagulation for small-gauge (23/25/27g) surgery unless extensive dissection is needed.
Orbital Surgery: High risk for sight-threatening hematoma; must coordinate with Hematology to bridge/stop anticoagulation.
DVT Prophylaxis: Use sequential compression devices (SCDs) for long orbital or plastic procedures (>90 mins).

rows: Inhibits Vit K dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X)

sections.title: Ocular Complications of Anticoagulants
content: Subconjunctival Hemorrhage (Benign but alarming to patients).
Spontaneous Hyphema (Rare, usually associated with underlying rubeosis).
Increased risk of vitreous hemorrhage in exudative AMD.
Progression of Sub-retinal hemorrhage in neovascular membranes.

sections.title: Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis (CST)
content: The Ocular Equivalent of DVT: Often septic (Staph aureus).
Signs: Proptosis, Chemosis, Cranial Nerve Palsies (III, IV, V1, V2, VI).
Key Finding: Rapid progression to bilateral involvement.
Treatment: High-dose IV antibiotics + Anticoagulation (controversial but often used).

branches: Baker's Cyst Rupture (Sudden pain, fluid in popliteal fossa)

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Phlegmasia Cerulea Dolens: A surgical emergency where massive DVT causes arterial compromise (blue, painful leg).
Post-Thrombotic Syndrome (PTS): Chronic venous hypertension causing leg heaviness and ulcers in 20-50% of DVT patients.
D-dimer Caveat: Elevated in pregnancy, cancer, and inflammation; only useful for its Negative Predictive Value.
Pre-op: Always document a baseline INR for patients on Warfarin before performing any needle-based anesthesia (e.g., retrobulbar block).

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Recent Advances
sections.content: The **EINSTEIN** and **AMPLIFY** trials revolutionized management by proving DOACs (Rivaroxaban and Apixaban) are non-inferior to Warfarin for DVT/PE treatment with a lower risk of major bleeding. In ophthalmology, recent retrospective series suggest that stopping DOACs for cataract surgery may actually increase the risk of systemic thromboembolism without significantly reducing surgical complications.
